Great — sounds like you’re excited! Based on what you’ve already been talking about (Strat vs Les Paul, open D tuning, coil-splits, and setup), here are practical things to look for when shopping at the music store this weekend:

- Play both types: try the Stratocaster and Les Paul (and any other models you like) so you can compare feel, weight, and tone in person. The passages you mentioned highlight clear differences in body/neck construction and feel, so hands‑on comparison matters.

- Pay attention to pickups and tonal options: Les Pauls typically have humbucking tones (warm, thick, good sustain). If you want more tonal flexibility, look for coil‑tap or coil‑splitting features — those give you more single‑coil–like sounds in addition to the Les Paul’s thicker voice.

- Feel and neck profile: notice the neck shape and how it fits your hand. Bolt‑on vs set necks and the neck profile will change playability — pick what feels comfortable for your fingerstyle, chords, and lead work.

- Weight and body construction: Les Pauls are heavier (mahogany/maple construction mentioned) and have a different balance than Strat‑style guitars; make sure the weight is comfortable for long playing sessions.

- Try acoustic‑style playing on electrics you’re considering: you asked whether a Les Paul can handle acoustic‑like fingerpicking (e.g., "Blackbird"); try the fingerpicked passages and see if the guitar’s tone and playability suit that style — some Les Pauls can work well for that.

- Setup and string choice: if you plan to use alternate tunings like open D, check how the guitar responds and ask about heavier string sets. Heavier gauges were recommended for open D to get fuller tone; also try different actions to see what works for your technique.

- Amp and settings: bring a short demo or ask to plug into an amp so you can judge the guitar’s sound in typical amp settings you like (the passages mention adjusting amp settings to get a good open D sound).

- Overall condition and hardware: if buying used, check the electronics (switches, pots), hardware condition, and that coil‑split (if present) functions correctly.

- Ask about setup options at purchase: if you like a guitar but want different action or string gauge, ask if the shop can set it up to your preferences.

- Bay count matters: 2-bay units are cheaper and simpler (good for starters), 4-bay gives more capacity and RAID flexibility for redundancy or future growth. Pick based on how much usable storage you’ll need and whether you want easier expansion.
- Ease of setup: as a beginner, look for a user-friendly NAS OS and good documentation/apps for backing up laptops and phones (Time Machine, Windows backups, mobile backup apps).
